prompt: How does every ASVS requirement begin?

choices.text: With the name of the attack it prevents
choices.why: ASVS describes what a well-built application does, not attacks.

choices.text: Verify that
choices.why: Right. A statement that is true or false of an application.

choices.text: With a severity score from 1 to 10
choices.why: Requirements carry a level, not a score.

choices.text: With the framework it applies to
choices.why: Requirements are independent of frameworks.

prompt: Why does the 'Verify that' shape matter?

choices.text: It makes the standard shorter
choices.why: Length is not the point.

choices.text: OWASP's lawyers require it
choices.why: Not a legal matter.

choices.text: Each requirement is checkable
choices.why: Right. 'The application is secure' cannot; a 'verify that' sentence can, by code, test or request.

choices.text: It lets tools fix the application automatically
choices.why: No tool fixes an application from a sentence.

prompt: Which level does the lesson give as Vereda's target, and why?

choices.text: Level 1, because it is the smallest
choices.why: Level 1 is the floor, met first, not the target.

choices.text: Level 2, because the portal holds health data
choices.why: Right. Level 2 is for applications handling personal data.

choices.text: Level 3, because health is involved and only the top level will do
choices.why: Level 3 is for the highest assurance; the lesson aims at 2.

choices.text: No level: small companies are exempt
choices.why: The standard exempts nobody; the level is a choice.

prompt: Which of these are true of ASVS? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: its levels are cumulative
choices.why: Level 2 includes every level 1 requirement.

choices.text: it is free and openly licensed
choices.why: OWASP's material is.

choices.text: meeting level 2 certifies an application as secure
choices.why: It says nothing about a flaw no requirement describes.

choices.text: it explains how to break applications
choices.why: It describes what a well-built one does.

prompt: ASVS 5.0.0 was released in May ___, replacing 4.0.3.
How many requirements does ASVS 5.0.0 contain in all?
How many requirements must an application meet in all to reach level 2?
Why does `python3 asvs.py v2.2.` end the prefix with a dot?

choices.text: Python requires a dot after arguments
choices.why: It does not.

choices.text: To search the chapter instead of the section
choices.why: The dot narrows, it does not widen.

choices.text: So V2.2 does not also match V2.20
choices.why: Right. A prefix without the dot would match longer section numbers.

choices.text: The CSV stores identifiers with a trailing dot
choices.why: It stores V2.2.1, with no trailing dot.

prompt: Match each ASVS chapter to its subject.
V2.2.2 says client-side validation 'must not be relied upon as a security control'. Which lesson taught the same thing?

choices.text: Lesson 4, escaping by context
choices.why: That one is about output.

choices.text: Lesson 3, where a form is a suggestion
choices.why: Right. A form is a suggestion; the server's check is the control.

choices.text: Lesson 17, dependencies and pinning
choices.why: That one is about packages.

choices.text: Lesson 19, the automated checks
choices.why: That one runs checks; lesson 3 argued this one.

prompt: In the identifier V2.2.1, the middle 2 names the ___ within chapter V2.
Match each lesson to the ASVS section it belongs to.
What does V7.4.1 require when a session is terminated?

choices.text: That the user is shown a goodbye page
choices.why: The page is not the point.

choices.text: That the session cannot be used again
choices.why: Right. For stateful sessions, invalidating the session data on the server.

choices.text: That the cookie is renamed
choices.why: Renaming does not stop the old one from working.

choices.text: That the password is changed automatically
choices.why: That is a different event.

prompt: V15.2.1 does not say 'no known vulnerabilities'. What does it say instead?

choices.text: Components must be the newest version on the day of release
choices.why: Not what it says, and not always wise.

choices.text: Components keep to documented update time frames
choices.why: Right. The project writes down how fast it acts on an advisory, and keeps to it.

choices.text: Only components from the standard library may be used
choices.why: Third-party components are expected.

choices.text: Every component must be audited by OWASP
choices.why: OWASP audits nobody's dependencies.

prompt: Lessons 18 and 19 map to no ASVS section of their own. Why?

choices.text: ASVS forbids code review
choices.why: It says nothing of the kind.

choices.text: They were added after ASVS was written
choices.why: Timing is not the reason.

choices.text: Automated testing is outside security
choices.why: It is how much of it is proved.

choices.text: They are how the other requirements are verified
choices.why: Right. A review and a test are the evidence, not a requirement of their own.

prompt: What does a cheat sheet give that ASVS deliberately leaves out?

choices.text: How to do it
choices.why: Right. ASVS says what; the cheat sheets say how.

choices.text: The list of requirements
choices.why: That is ASVS itself.

choices.text: A certificate of compliance
choices.why: Neither project issues one.

choices.text: The level an application must meet
choices.why: Choosing the level is the team's decision.

prompt: Match each lesson to its cheat sheet.
Which habit does the lesson recommend when reading a cheat sheet?

choices.text: Read it end to end before writing any code
choices.why: Slower, and it sticks less.

choices.text: Copy its example into the project unchanged
choices.why: Translate it into your framework's call first.

choices.text: Go to it with a question
choices.why: Right. The answer is usually a paragraph.

choices.text: Trust a recent blog post over it
choices.why: The sheet is reviewed and updated; the post may not be.

prompt: Put the working pattern the lesson gives in order.
items: write a test that states it
make it pass the way the cheat sheet says
keep the test, so it stays true

prompt: A checklist line says `met` and gives no evidence. What does the lesson call it?

choices.text: Acceptable at level 1, where evidence is optional
choices.why: Evidence is asked at every level.

choices.text: A belief, not a status
choices.why: Right. The evidence is a test name, a configuration file or a check.

choices.text: Compliance, in the sense auditors use
choices.why: Compliance without evidence is a claim.

choices.text: Not applicable
choices.why: That is a different status.

prompt: Where does the lesson say to start working through the checklist?

choices.text: At V1, in alphabetical order
choices.why: Order of risk, not of numbering.

choices.text: At the shortest chapter
choices.why: Size is not risk.

choices.text: Where a failure would expose others' data
choices.why: Right. Authorisation, sessions, validation and encoding first.

choices.text: At level 3, to aim high
choices.why: Level 1 first, then the target level.

prompt: V7.4.1 says a terminated session cannot be used. What test turns it into evidence?

choices.text: One that signs in and checks the welcome page shows the name
choices.why: That proves sign-in works, not termination.

choices.text: Sign out, replay the old cookie, expect a refusal
choices.why: Right. The requirement becomes a refusal a test can state.

choices.text: One that counts the cookies in the browser
choices.why: The browser is not where the session ends.

choices.text: A bandit scan of the logout route
choices.why: No risky call to find; it is behaviour.

prompt: When does the lesson say to review the checklist? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: when a feature lands in a section it covers
choices.why: The section's status may change.

choices.text: when a new ASVS version is released
choices.why: Requirements may change.

choices.text: never, once every line is met
choices.why: A checklist goes stale like a pin.

choices.text: only before an external audit
choices.why: Then it would be wrong the rest of the year.

prompt: A manager asks whether the portal 'passed ASVS'. Which answer fits the lesson?

choices.text: Yes: bandit and pip-audit are green
choices.why: Two tools cover a handful of requirements.

choices.text: ASVS cannot be passed by a web application
choices.why: It can meet a level; that is what levels are for.

choices.text: It meets N of the 253 level 2 requirements; here is the evidence
choices.why: Right. A level, a count and evidence per line, not a yes.

choices.text: Yes, since no vulnerability was reported this year
choices.why: Absence of reports is not evidence of meeting requirements.

prompt: A requirement is about documenting how the application handles files. How is it met?

choices.text: With a document
choices.why: Right. Some requirements are about documentation and become a document, not a test.

choices.text: With a unit test of the upload route
choices.why: The requirement asks for documentation.

choices.text: It is level 3, so the portal ignores it
choices.why: V5.1.1 is level 2.

choices.text: By scanning the code with bandit
choices.why: No scanner reads documentation.

prompt: Why is the chosen ASVS level recorded in the repository with who decided?

choices.text: OWASP requires a signed form from each project that uses it
choices.why: OWASP requires nothing of anybody.

choices.text: It is a promise the work measures itself against
choices.why: Right. A decision with an owner, like the risk decisions of lessons 17 and 18.

choices.text: git cannot work without it
choices.why: git does not care.

choices.text: So the level can be lowered quietly later, when it gets in the way
choices.why: Recording it does the opposite.
